beats.act: Open the Library
beats.say: The Library is the parts bin: skills, hooks, connections, templates, and what the community has published. It is not a dashboard — every shelf on it is something an agent composes.

beats.act: Press "+ New skill"
beats.say: A skill is a reusable instruction packet — the unit an agent composes to know how to do something. This page offers two ways to make one, and the operator is about to take the one that does not involve typing markdown.

beats.act: Describe the skill to the creation agent instead of writing the package by hand
beats.say: This is the fork in the road, and both branches are real: the operator can type the package into the form beside this one, or describe what they want and let the creation agent draft it. Same library, same scan, same approval — different amount of typing.

do.with: A skill that checks every relative link in a markdown file resolves to a real path in the repo, and reports the ones that do not with their line numbers.

beats.act: Open the authoring session it just started
beats.say: Forge mints the session and says so on the page the operator is already standing on, rather than moving them somewhere they did not ask to go. Reaching it is the operator’s own next act.

beats.act: Read what it drafted, give the package its directory name, and approve it
beats.say: The agent drafts; the operator names and approves. Nothing an agent wrote enters the library on the agent’s own say-so, and the id the operator types is the directory it lands in — as a draft, which is not the same as trusted.

beats.act: Trust it: approve the draft in the library
beats.say: Two approvals, because they answer different questions. The first says the draft is finished; this one says you trust it enough to let an agent load it. Until this press the package is installed, quarantined and invisible to every palette — which is what a trust gate is for.

beats.act: Go back to the Library
beats.say: The Library is where the operator returns between kinds. Each shelf is a different sort of part, and the next one is the only sort that is executable code.

beats.act: Press "+ New hook"
beats.say: A hook is the other kind of part: not instructions but a script, run on an agent’s lifecycle event. It is the only thing in the library that is executable code, which is why it is the only thing with a security gate in front of it.

beats.act: Write the hook by hand: what it runs on, what it does, and what it may touch
beats.say: The permissions fields are the operator declaring, up front, what this script is allowed to reach. They are also what the scanner checks the script against — a behaviour the manifest declares is still counted, because the declaration is written by whoever wrote the script.

do.with: Note that a session ended, so the ledger has something to show.

beats.act: Read the security scan before trusting it
beats.say: This is the gate that exists because a hook runs with the operator’s own credentials. The scan is static, it is shown before the approval and not after, and a declared behaviour is downgraded but still counted — never hidden.

beats.act: Check what is actually in the package — every file, and the fingerprint over all of them
beats.say: Approving bytes you were never shown is not approving. The page lists every file in the package with its own hash and the fingerprint over the set, so a sibling script the entry point quietly sources cannot ride along unseen.

beats.act: Approve the hook
beats.say: Trust and verdict are two different axes, and this is the trust one. Approved and runnable is the state that lets an agent carry it; until the operator pressed this, the hook was a file on disk that nothing would ever execute.

beats.act: Test-fire the approved hook, before any agent carries it
beats.say: Approval is a promise about bytes; a test-fire is the bytes running. The hook executes here through the same gate a real dispatch uses, and the page records the run — when, on which event, and how it ended — while still saying plainly that nothing will fire it on its own until an agent carries it.

beats.act: Go back to the Library once more
beats.say: Third kind, same parts bin.

beats.act: Press "+ New template" and write the template the hook’s output is filed into
beats.say: A template is one markdown definition file — the shape an artifact comes out in. It is the least dramatic thing in the library and the one that decides whether two runs produce comparable output.

beats.act: Back to the Library
beats.say: Instructions are the fourth kind of part, and their door now sits in the parts bin with the other three.

beats.act: Open the instructions launcher straight from the Library
beats.say: One click from the parts bin to the launcher. The story walks it rather than teleporting, because an operator cannot teleport.

beats.act: Draft the project’s own working instructions, so the parts have a house style to follow
beats.say: Instructions are the fourth kind of component and the only one that is about the project rather than about forge: the AGENTS.md every agent dispatched at this repo reads before it does anything.

beats.act: Open the instructions session it just started
beats.say: Same shape as the skill: forge mints the session and says so where the operator already is, and reaching it is their own next act.

beats.act: Head back to the Agents pillar
beats.say: The parts are all made now — a skill, a hook, a template, a house style. None of them does anything yet. Binding happens on a worker’s own page, and the way back to a worker is the Agents pillar.

beats.act: Open brain-ingest from the roster
beats.say: The roster is a list of workers; binding happens on one worker’s own page. This is the hop the operator makes without thinking about it, and the one the story forgot to write down.

beats.act: Bind the hook to the agent, and save it
beats.say: A hook is inert until an agent carries it. Binding is the act that makes a library part part of a worker, and it is the reason the hook’s own page counts how many agents carry it.

beats.act: Run the agent
beats.say: The hook is bound, so this run is the first time anything other than the operator can set it off. It fires on the session ending — so the story waits for the ending.

beats.act: Wait for the run to end
beats.say: A session that ends is the event this hook was written for. Until the run finishes there is nothing to fire on.

beats.act: Back to the Library
beats.say: The record of what a hook did lives with the hook, not with whichever agent happened to trigger it.

beats.act: Open the hook, and see the session ending fire it
beats.say: This is where S7 ends: the hook the operator wrote, scanned, approved and bound actually ran, and its own page says when and how it ended. A hook nobody can prove fired is a hook nobody should trust — this one has a record.
